summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts handling domestic affairs. Danish legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies here, so a visitor's legal position on those questions follows the Danish framework as received in Greenland.

The sources record no criminal penalty for same-sex relations. Since 2010 Article 100 of the Criminal Code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the Code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No reported cases of prosecution under these provisions appear in the inventory.

Same-sex marriage has been in effect since 1 April 2016, adopted from a Danish bill passed unanimously on two occasions after the first attempt lapsed through elections. It replaced the registered partnership regime (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) that had run from 1 July 1996 until the marriage law took effect, and the bishop of the established church supported the change. The 1996 partnership law itself had passed with virtually no debate.

Transgender visitors and residents can change the sex designation on official identity documents. A law adopted by decree in 2016 allows legal sex change on the basis of self-determination, with no requirement for sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or a medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18, state that they want their documentation changed, and observe a six-month reflection period before the request is confirmed. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor alongside male and female.

Greenland's parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, in force from 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics among other characteristics. The law establishes an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
Accounts of social life describe homosexuality as low-key, integrated and non-violent, with gay life characterised as "almost a non-event" in public terms. Public expression became visible with the first pride parade in Nuuk on 15 May 2010, attended by roughly 1,000 people, and a modest Pride march has been held annually since 2010.

There is virtually no organised gay scene, a consequence of the small and scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd. In August 2014 the national association LGBT Qaamaneq was founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, working for political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.
localsOnly:
Discrimination complaints under the 2024 Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination are managed by the Equal Treatment Board, while the Equality Council is charged with promoting non-discrimination. These are the resident-facing routes for pursuing a claim on grounds that include gender identity and gender expression.

The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights in the territory.

The legal sex change procedure requires only an application by a person over 18 and a six-month reflection period, with no medical or surgical preconditions, after which the sex designation on identity documents is updated.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no reported prosecutions under Article 100 or under the hate-crime penalty enhancement, and no data on how often police or prosecutors pursue such cases; enforcement frequency remains unresolved on this evidence.

No sourced material was available on toilet or facility rules, healthcare access for transgender travellers, immigration or border screening questions that could disclose gender history, or recognition of foreign documents and foreign marriages at the point of entry.

Whether Greenland applies any Danish provisions on legal capacity, sterilisation or parental status that were not covered by the 2016 decree is not resolved in these sources.
